pages.label: ii
pages.text: e Figure 1: The programme progresses through core concepts, method building, cumulative projects and reusable research outputs. Research software, reproducibility and documentation support all four stages. This programme is a staged path from concepts to reusable scientific outputs. The aim is not to accumulate disconnected topics, but to learn how explanation, computation, uncertainty, validation, and software practice combine into defensible research work. ii

pages.label: iii
pages.text: e The big picture: one evidence loop Figure 2: Define the scientific question, build a representation, compute predictions, compare with evidence, assess uncertainty, then decide and revise. Scientific software supports every stage. The whole book is organized around one recurring question: what would make a computational scientific claim defensible? A claim is defensible only if the scientific question, the representation, the computation, the evidence, the uncertainty analysis, and the final decision all remain visible. None of these layers can substitute for the others. This is why the book does not treat AI as an isolated add-on and does not hide software engineering in an appendix. A neural surrogate can change the meaning of mechanistic parameters; an observation model can determine practical identifiability; a discretization can create or suppress dynamics; a software interface can silently change units. The evidence loop is therefore both a scientific workflow and a curriculum map. iii

pages.label: iv
pages.text: e iv / 413 Using the worked lessons Each chapter now starts with a teaching sequence: a concrete question, definitions, explicit calculations, an executable example, interpretation, and two practice problems. The calculations are in teaching/ examples/; their saved numerical outputs are in teaching/results/. The 54 practice problems have fully worked solutions in Appendix A. The later research investigations extend these examples. Their diagnostic guides are not complete empirical studies and are labelled separately. Begin with the worked calculation when a concept is unfamiliar; move to the open investigation after you can reproduce and explain the small case. Familiarity with mechanistic modelling does not imply familiarity with every statistical or computational method. A quick glossary before the chapters Term Plain-language definition and why it matters Model A controlled abstraction of a real system, built for a specific question. A model is not reality in miniature; it is a simplification whose assumptions must stay visible. State variable A quantity the model evolves internally, such as biomass, concentration, or volt- age. States are often not observed directly. Parameter A quantity that controls the behaviour of the model without being updated by the model dynamics, such as a rate constant or elastic modulus. Observable A measured quantity or derived output connected to the internal state by an observation function. Confusing states with observables is a major source of false confidence. Inverse problem The task of inferring unknown states, parameters, inputs, or structure from obser- vations. Most model fitting is an inverse problem. Identifiability The question of whether the available data can uniquely constrain the unknown quantities. A parameter can be numerically estimated without being scientifically identifiable. Conditioning The sensitivity of the mathematical answer to small perturbations in the in- puts. Poor conditioning means tiny errors in data or coefficients can cause large changes in the inferred answer. Regularization An explicit way to stabilize or constrain an inverse problem when the data do not support every direction equally. It is not just a numerical trick; it changes the information geometry of the problem. Prior / posterior In Bayesian inference, the prior encodes assumptions before seeing current data, while the posterior updates those assumptions after combining them with the likelihood from observed data. Uncertainty propaga- tion The step where uncertainty in parameters, states, or inputs is pushed forward to the scientific quantity of interest. Decision-relevant uncertainty lives in the outputs, not only in parameter tables. Validation The process of checking whether a model or learned system is adequate for its intended scientific use. Validation is broader than goodness of fit. Reproducibility The ability for another person or future you to rerun, inspect, and verify the com- putational chain. Reproducibility supports trust but does not, by itself, prove scientific correctness. How to work through the book Read actively. For a new method, first identify the scientific question and the minimal example. Then follow the derivation, inspect the figure, run or adapt the code, and finish by stating what evidence would falsify the method on a real problem. Problems are collected at the ends of chapters so that explanation Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

pages.label: v
pages.text: e v / 413 remains readable. External resources are used as active studios: when a chapter points to BioModels, PEtab, SALib, PyMC, SciML, BEIR or The Turing Way, the task is to reproduce, inspect, modify, or evaluate something specific rather than merely browse a link. The course uses three levels of evidence repeatedly. First, verify a method on a case where the answer or qualitative behavior is known. Second, move to a community benchmark where implementations can be compared. Third, move to a real scientific dataset or model where the ground truth is incomplete and model criticism becomes part of the work. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

pages.text: e How examples, exercises, hints, and solu- tions work in this edition The intended learning progression is worked reasoning, a guided investigation, staged hints, a reference comparison and a project artifact. These are distinct evidence levels. The research-investigation appendix provides 44 diagnostic guides; not every guide is a fully closed computational investigation. The four tumour reference notebooks and their results now form one completed, bounded synthetic chain, reproduced in Chapter 26. Other supplied examples are labeled by their demonstrated scope rather than by the amount of advice they contain. Use learner templates before opening the reference. A template that raises NotImplementedError is intentionally unfinished; a passing import test is not evidence that its scientific exercise has been solved. Each main learner project now includes executable acceptance checks and domain-specific interfaces in exercise.py. x

pages.label: xii
pages.text: e How to use the examples Start with the worked lesson at the beginning of the relevant chapter. Each lesson defines its mathematical objects, fixes numerical inputs, carries out calculations, and explains what the result permits you to conclude. Run the matching teaching/examples/chNN.py module from the package root and compare its output with the saved JSON result. The small example is a reference you can understand completely, not a claim that the real research problem is equally simple. The remainder of the chapter develops related methods and open investigations. The four synthetic reference cases demonstrate complete numerical workflows; research transfer requires the actual model, data rights, observation process, and collaborators’ contribution records. Work the two practice questions before reading their solutions. A solution explains the intermediate reasoning and the meaning of the result; it is not merely a final number. Change one assumption or input after reproducing the reference calculation and predict what will change before rerunning the code. xii

pages.label: xiii
pages.text: e Reading the figures Quantitative plots identify their axes, units or dimensionless coordinates, and declared example. Their data come from the accompanying calculations. Schematic diagrams illustrate an explicitly described operation; they are not empirical evidence. A caption states how to read the comparison and where its interpretation stops. The cover and the three programme-overview illustrations use the selected artwork from the supplied design reference. They are editorial illustrations, not measured data. They are included as complete source assets, without surrounding page text or clipped panels. Technical plots and computational diagrams retain the typeset vector artwork and calculations from the worked V6.17 edition. Related comparisons are separated when combining them would hide the operation being taught. The figure register and design-provenance record in the package distinguish these two roles. xiii

C CHAPTER 1 Scientific Models as Executable Arguments ◎Learning objectives • scientific contracts • observation/noise separation • limiting-case verification ☼Pedagogical objective Make the learner treat a model as an executable scientific argument rather than a collection of equations. ¨ Project link MultiScaleTwin / TumorTherapyTwin: model contract, observables, invari- ant tests. 1.1 From a physical question to an equation you can check A model is a deliberately restricted representation of a system. Its usefulness is judged against a question, not against the impossible requirement of reproducing everything. A mechanistic model specifies processes that change quantities: transport, reaction, birth, death, heat exchange, or a decision rule. An empirical curve can be useful without making those mechanistic commitments. Neither label establishes accuracy by itself. Before reading the general notation below, consider a reservoir. Material enters at a constant rate and each unit already present has a constant chance per unit time of leaving. We want the amount remaining after a change in the input. This modest question is sufficient to introduce states, parameters, forcing, initial conditions, observations, units, numerical solutions and verification. The same distinctions will reappear in a lipid pool or a leaf water store; the reservoir does not by itself validate either biological application. Worked example 1: build a balance, rather than guess a curve Let X(t) be the amount in the reservoir, in milligrams, and let t be time in hours. The input q = 2 has units mg h−1. The removal coefficient k = 0.4 has units h−1. Thus kX is a removal rate, not an amount. Over a small interval ∆t, the change is approximately X(t + ∆t) −X(t) ≃q∆t −kX(t)∆t. Divide by ∆t and take the limiting rate of change: dX dt = q −kX, X(0) = 1. 2

Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 3 / 413 X is a state variable: the equation evolves it. k is a parameter: it specifies the removal mechanism in this model. q is a constant forcing; in another experiment it could be a prescribed function q(t). The equilibrium, written X∗, is a state with zero derivative. Setting 0 = q −kX∗gives X∗= q/k = 5 mg. This is not an instruction to set X to five immediately. Substitution gives ˙Z = −kZ, so separation of variables gives Z(t) = Z(0)e−kt. Therefore X(t) = 5 −4e−0.4t. At one hour, X(1) ≃2.31872 mg; at two hours, X(2) ≃3.20268 mg. The time constant 1/k = 2.5 h is the time for the deviation from equilibrium to fall by a factor e. It is not the time to reach equilibrium exactly. Worked example 2: a falling concentration need not mean material is disappearing An instrument often reports concentration C = X/V , rather than total amount X. Suppose X = 10 mg is conserved but the volume grows as V (t) = 2 + t litres. Then C(t) = 10 2 + t, dC dt = − 10 (2 + t)2 . The concentrations at t = 0, 1, 2 h are 5, 10/3 and 2.5 mg per litre, even though no material has left. A model that interprets this concentration decline as chemical degradation will infer a process that is not present. The quotient rule explains the missing term in general: ˙C = ˙X V −X ˙V V 2 = ˙X V −C ˙V V . The second term is dilution. The distinction matters for growing cells, expanding tissue, fluid compart- ments and changing leaf water content. C Chapter 1. Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 5 / 413 Scientific modelling is treated as evidence engineering: representation, observation, computation, and software are separate but coupled layers. 1.2 A model is an executable scientific argument The central object in this book is not an equation, an estimator, a neural network, or a software package. It is a scientific claim whose chain of support can be inspected. A model states which entities exist, how they interact, which quantities are observed, which processes are ignored, and under what conditions its predictions should be trusted. Computation then turns those commitments into consequences. Data confront those consequences. Software preserves the chain well enough that another person can inspect it. This framing changes how we read every later chapter. A good fit is not automatically good evidence. A converged solver is not automatically a correct discretization. A calibrated classifier is not automatically transportable. A reproducible repository is not automatically scientifically valid. Each layer has a different failure mode, and the job of the computational scientist is to keep them separated long enough to diagnose them. 1.2.1 Study a real curation workflow before writing your own model The BioModels training material is a useful model of what “model correctness” means in practice. BioModels distinguishes literature-derived mechanistic models from automatically generated resources and describes curation as checking the encoded structure against the publication, verifying parameters and units, and reproducing published behavior with an independent simulator. See https://www. ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/biomodels-quick-tour/ and the BioModels FAQ at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biomodels/faq. Do not merely browse the site. Choose one curated model and reconstruct a one-page scientific contract: biological scope, state variables, parameters, observables, units, initial conditions, interventions, and the exact published behavior that curation reproduces. Then identify at least three claims that the SBML file cannot establish by itself. This exercise establishes the standard used throughout the book: representation, evidence, and computation are distinct objects. 1.3 A model is a controlled abstraction A mechanistic model is not a miniature copy of reality. It is a deliberately simplified causal representation built for a question. The same biological system can require different models depending on whether the objective is explanation, prediction, parameter inference, control, extrapolation, or experimental design. A useful modelling statement has five parts: system + scale + question + assumptions + observables. (1.1) For example, “model photosynthesis” is underspecified. A stronger formulation is: predict leaf carbon assimilation over minute-to-hour environmental variation using biochemical and stomatal processes, assuming spatially homogeneous leaf properties and quasi-steady intracellular intermediates, with gas-exchange measurements as observables. The formulation determines which mechanisms belong in the model. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

C Chapter 1. Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 6 / 413 1.3.1 Mechanistic versus phenomenological A mechanistic component aims to represent a process through hypothesized causal structure. A phe- nomenological component represents an empirical relationship without necessarily claiming the under- lying mechanism. The distinction is not binary. The Michaelis–Menten form v(S) = VmaxS Km + S (1.2) can be mechanistically derived under specific assumptions, yet it is also frequently used phenomenologi- cally when those assumptions are not verified. Therefore, ask not only “is this equation mechanistic?” but: • Which variables have physical/biological meaning? • Which relationships arise from conservation or known kinetics? • Which terms are closures or empirical approximations? • Which assumptions are required for the derivation? • Which parameters can be transferred outside the calibration context? 1.3.2 State variables and observables are different Let the latent mechanistic state be x(t) and measured data be y(t). A general state-space formulation is ˙x = f(x, u, p, t), (1.3) y = h(x, p) + ϵ. (1.4) The observation function h matters. Experiments rarely measure every model state directly. Ignoring the measurement process can create false identifiability. Two internal states may influence the same observable combination, making them impossible to infer separately even if the ODE solution itself is unique. 1.4 Conservation laws before equations A strong modelling habit is to start from balances. For an amount X in a compartment, dX dt = inflows −outflows + production −consumption. (1.5) This structure prevents many sign and bookkeeping errors. For a concentration c = X/V , changing volume introduces additional terms: dc dt = 1 V dX dt −X V 2 dV dt . (1.6) Treating concentration dynamics as amount dynamics without accounting for volume change can be scientifically wrong. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

C Chapter 1. Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 7 / 413 1.4.1 Dimensions as an error detector Every additive term in an equation must have the same physical dimensions. If dx dt = k1x −k2xy, (1.7) then the dimensions of k1 and k2 must make both right-hand terms have dimension [x]/[t]. Dimensional analysis cannot prove a model correct, but it can prove many equations wrong. 1.4.2 Nondimensionalization reveals structure Suppose ˙X = aX −bXY, (1.8) ˙Y = cXY −dY. (1.9) Choose characteristic scales X0 = d/c, Y0 = a/b, and τ = at. Define x = X/X0, y = Y/Y0. Then dx dτ = x(1 −y), (1.10) dy dτ = ρy(x −1), ρ = d a. (1.11) Four dimensional parameters collapse to one dimensionless ratio ρ. This tells you which combinations control qualitative behavior and can illuminate identifiability. 1.4.3 Timescales A process with rate constant k has characteristic timescale roughly τ ∼1 k. (1.12) If one process acts on milliseconds and another on hours, treating them identically can create stiffness and may suggest model reduction. If τfast ≪τslow, a fast variable may approximately satisfy a quasi-steady relation. But the approximation needs justification; transients or perturbations can invalidate it. 1.4.4 Scale is more than spatial size Multiscale systems can involve different: • spatial scales; • temporal scales; • organizational scales; • modelling representations; • data resolutions. A molecular event, cell response, tissue transport process, organism phenotype, and environmental driver can have qualitatively different state representations. C Chapter 1. Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 8 / 413 Multiscale modelling is therefore not “one huge ODE.” It is the principled coupling of representations whose assumptions may differ. 1.4.5 Where ML belongs Machine learning is most valuable when it addresses a specific limitation. Typical roles include: 1. surrogate: approximate an expensive mechanistic simulator; 2. closure: learn an unresolved process or scale coupling; 3. observation model: map high-dimensional measurements to mechanistic states; 4. inference accelerator: amortize parameter or state estimation; 5. representation learning: compress complex data while retaining predictive structure; 6. model discrepancy: represent systematic mismatch between mechanistic prediction and data; 7. experimental policy: choose informative experiments or simulations. The question is not “can a neural network fit this?” but “what epistemic role should the learned component play?” 1.4.6 A hybrid decomposition One generic hybrid dynamical model is ˙x = fknown(x, p) + gθ(x, u), (1.13) where fknown encodes trusted mechanisms and gθ represents an unresolved contribution. This structure can preserve conservation, monotonicity, or other constraints if designed carefully. It also provides a scientific interpretation: the neural component is not “the model”; it is a specified missing term. Failure to watch. A flexible learned residual can absorb errors from incorrect parameters, wrong initial conditions, missing measurement effects, or structural model defects. Excellent predictive fit does not automatically identify the missing mechanism. 1.4.7 Model complexity should answer a question Add a state, parameter, or learned component only if it improves something relevant: • resolves a falsified assumption; • represents a new experimental intervention; • improves out-of-sample prediction meaningfully; • allows a scientifically important latent quantity to be estimated; • connects a scale required by the research question; • reduces systematic model discrepancy with defensible structure. If complexity only improves in-sample fit, it may be compensating for noise. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

C Chapter 1. Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 9 / 413 Write a two-page modelling specification for a current research problem before touching ML. Include scale diagram, equations or balance structure, observables, uncertainties, candidate learned components, and at least one reason not to use ML for part of the system. 1.5 The five contracts A reusable mechanistic model should separate five objects. 1. State contract: what variables carry memory and require initial conditions? 2. Flux/process contract: what physical, chemical, or biological processes change those states? 3. Forcing/intervention contract: what enters from outside the modeled dynamics? 4. Observation contract: how does a state trajectory become a measured quantity? 5. Noise/discrepancy contract: what variation is assigned to measurement noise, process noise, and model inadequacy? Confusing these layers causes common inferential failures. A fluorescence measurement is not a molecular concentration merely because it is monotone in that concentration. A fitted scaling factor belongs to an observation model unless the underlying mechanism justifies interpreting it as a biological rate. 1.5.1 Balance laws before kinetics For an amount ni in a control volume, dni dt = X j Sijvj(n, θ, u, t) + qin i −qout i . The stoichiometric matrix S encodes what each process changes; the rate laws vj encode how fast those processes occur. Keeping topology and kinetics separate makes conservation analysis, parameter interpretation, and model extension much cleaner.  Worked analysis: 1: two-compartment pharmacokinetics Let Ac, Ap be drug amounts in central and peripheral compartments. Verify by summing the equations. This simple symbolic check should become an executable regression test. C Chapter 1. Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 13 / 413 Failure to watch: adding biological detail without information. A more mechanistic model can be less scientifically useful if the available measurements cannot distinguish its new parameters or states. Mechanistic plausibility and inferential identifiability are separate properties. Add detail only when it changes a scientific question and can be constrained, bounded, or tested. 1.9.1 Dimensional and limiting-case checks Every rate term must have state-per-time units. Beyond dimensional consistency, use limiting cases. If substrate goes to zero, should a flux vanish? If a resistance goes to infinity, should transport stop? If temperature effects are removed, should the model reduce to the reference formulation? Limiting cases are high-value tests because they encode scientific expectations that survive refactoring. Create model_contract.md, an SBML/PEtab-compatible separation of model/conditions/observables where feasible, and invariant/limiting-case tests. Do this before adding inference or ML. 1.10 Source criticism precedes reproduction The source model is evidence to inspect, not an authority that can override arithmetic. In the supplied tumour paper, Table 1 gives b = 3.17 × 10−6, µ = 2.0 × 10−2 and α2 = 6.41 × 10−11. The reduced equation prints the coefficient bµ/α2 as 0.018. C CHAPTER 2 Linear Algebra, Information Geometry, and Inverse Problems ◎Learning objectives • conditioning and singular directions • least-squares geometry • regularization as an information decision ☼Pedagogical objective Connect linear algebra to the geometry of inverse problems rather than teaching matrix routines in isolation. ¨ Project link NumeriCore + inference tracks: conditioning diagnostics and regularized baselines. 2.1 Learn the inverse problem through two measurements A matrix is more than a rectangular container of numbers. Multiplication by a matrix describes how an input vector is transformed into an output vector. In an experiment, the input can be a collection of unknown quantities and the output a collection of measured signals. The dimensions of the matrix therefore tell us what is being connected: a matrix with m rows and n columns maps n unknown coordinates to m observation coordinates. A forward problem computes observations from specified unknowns. An inverse problem tries to infer those unknowns from the observations. Reversing the direction can turn a harmless small coefficient into a dangerous division by a small number. We will calculate that effect before using terms such as conditioning or singular value. Worked example 1: where noise amplification comes from Consider two standardized unknowns x1, x2 and measurements y1 = x1, y2 = 0.01x2, or y = Ax, A = 1 0 0 0.01  . If the true vector is (1, 1)T , the noiseless observation is (1, 0.01)T . Suppose an error of 0.10 is added to the second observation. The recorded vector is then (1, 0.11)T . Exact inversion gives bx1 = 1, bx2 = 0.11/0.01 = 11. 14

C Chapter 2. Linear Algebra, Information Geometry, and Inverse Problems 15 / 413 The algorithm can be perfectly implemented and still infer eleven where the generating value was one. The observed error has been amplified by a factor of 100 in that direction. The condition number compares the largest and smallest directional amplification of a nonsingular linear map. Here it is 1/0.01 = 100 in the Euclidean norm. It describes the sensitivity of the mathematical problem, not an error in the programming language. Changing the solver cannot recover information that the measurement barely contains. The two coordinate directions in this diagonal example are already its right singular vectors. Their amplification factors, one and 0.01, are its singular values. For a general matrix these special directions may be mixtures of the original coordinates. The singular-value decomposition, A = UΣV T , rotates into those directions, scales them, and rotates to the observation coordinates. A singular value close to zero identifies a direction whose effect is difficult to distinguish from measurement noise. A singular value exactly zero identifies a direction that has no effect in the linear map. Worked example 2: regularization is a calculable compromise Regularization means adding a stated preference or constraint when data alone make the inverse answer unstable or nonunique. For standardized coordinates, ridge regularization penalizes squared coefficient size: J(x1, x2) = (x1 −1)2 + (0.01x2 −0.11)2 + α(x2 1 + x2 2). The first two terms measure disagreement with the data. The last term penalizes large unknown values. The tuning parameter α ≥0 determines how strongly that preference acts. The units and scaling of the residual and penalty have to be specified before α can be interpreted. Take the two derivatives separately: ∂J ∂x1 = 2(x1 −1) + 2αx1, ∂J ∂x2 = 2(0.01)(0.01x2 −0.11) + 2αx2. Setting them to zero gives bx1 = 1 1 + α, bx2 = 0.0011 0.0001 + α. For α = 0.01, these are approximately 0.99010 and 0.10891. The large estimate of eleven has disappeared, but we have not magically recovered the true second value of one. The regularizer has strongly favoured a small second coefficient because the second measurement is weak. With α = 0.0001, the second estimate is 5.5 instead. These different answers expose the assumptions added by the penalty. This is the bias–variance trade-off in concrete form. Bias is systematic displacement of an estimator’s average from the generating quantity. Variance is the estimator’s fluctuation across repeated noisy datasets. Shrinking the weak direction adds bias but may greatly reduce its fluctuations. Whether that trade-off is acceptable depends on the scientific use; a stable answer is not necessarily a well-identified mechanism. For implementation, rewrite the objective as an ordinary least-squares problem with extra rows:  A √αI  x − y 0  2 2 . The new rows encode the penalty. The routine ridge in teaching/core.py solves this augmented problem with numpy.linalg.lstsq; it does not form an explicit matrix inverse. C Chapter 2. Linear Algebra, Information Geometry, and Inverse Problems 16 / 413 -m teaching.examples.ch02 prints all four penalty choices, making the algebra directly checkable. Worked example 3: a nonunique answer is different from a noisy answer Suppose the measurements are y1 = x1 + x2 and y2 = 2x1 + 2x2. The second measurement repeats the first combination. If the data are (2, 4)T , then (1, 1)T , (0, 2)T and (3, −1)T all reproduce them exactly. Positivity would remove some possibilities but not distinguish the first two. The direction (1, −1)T belongs to the null space: adding any multiple of it leaves both observations unchanged. The matrix has rank one, because it provides only one independent observation direction. Ridge regularization can choose one representative, but the data have not acquired a second independent direction. Now change the second equation to y2 = x1 + 1.01x2. With observations (2, 2.01) the unique solution is (1, 1). With observations (2, 2.02) it is (0, 2). The matrix is full rank, but a change of 0.01 in one measured number changes each inferred component by one. This is practical difficulty caused by weak information, rather than exact nonuniqueness. In nonlinear models, structural identifiability concerns uniqueness under an ideal observation specification; practical identifiability concerns what the actual noisy experiment can constrain. Neither is established solely by optimizer convergence. From numbers to code and experimental design 1 truth = np.array([1.0, 1.0]) 2 observed = A @ truth + np.array([0.0, 0.1]) 3 fits = {str(a): ridge(A, observed, a).tolist() for a in [0.0, 0.0001, 0.01, 0.1]} 4 S = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [2.0, 2.0]]) 5 null = np.array([1.0, -1.0]) / np.sqrt(2) 6 near = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.01]]) 7 result = {’A’: A.tolist(), ’observed’: observed.tolist(), ’truth’: truth.tolist(), ’ fits’: fits, ’null_residual’: (S @ null).tolist(), ’unperturbed’: np.linalg.solve(near, [2.0, 2.01]).tolist(), ’perturbed’: np.linalg.solve(near, [2.0, 2.02]).tolist()} 8 print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, default=_encode_numeric)) 9 if __name__ == ’__main__’: 10 main() Every column of A describes the observation response to one unknown. Every row describes one measurement. This row–column interpretation is what you should carry into a sensitivity matrix. The raw numerical singular values are meaningful only after deciding how parameters are scaled and how observation noise is weighted. This Jacobian-vector product (JVP) computes how outputs change under one input perturbation direction without forming the full Jacobian. It does not directly give the state at future times. A numerical method replaces that continuous evolution with a sequence of calculations. The replacement introduces error even when every line of code is correct. Three ideas must remain separate. Accuracy concerns closeness to the desired solution. Stability concerns whether the numerical recurrence magnifies disturbances in an unacceptable way. Consistency concerns whether the local approximation approaches the differential equation as the step tends to zero. A stable answer can be inaccurate, and a formally accurate method can behave disastrously when used outside its stability regime. Worked example 1: construct explicit Euler from a slope For ˙x = −4x and x(0) = 1, the exact solution is x(t) = e−4t. Explicit Euler uses the slope at the beginning of each step: xn+1 = xn + h(−4xn) = (1 −4h)xn. With h = 0.1, the first values are 1, 0.6, 0.36 and 0.216. The exact values at t = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 are approximately 0.67032, 0.44933 and 0.30119. Euler decays too quickly here. The state remains positive, but positivity is not accuracy. The multiplier 1 −4h determines the behaviour of this recurrence. For h = 0.4, the multiplier is −0.6: magnitudes decay while the sign alternates, although the true solution is always positive. For h = 0.6, 54

Stability for this scalar decay test requires |1 −4h| < 1, or 0 < h < 0.5. Nonnegative iterates require the stricter h ≤0.25. This calculation gives a reason for a time-step restriction. It does not establish the stability of every nonlinear equation; it provides a local warning when large negative rates are present. Worked example 2: implicit Euler changes the algebraic task Implicit Euler evaluates the right-hand side at the unknown end of the step: xn+1 = xn −4hxn+1. Collecting terms gives (1 + 4h)xn+1 = xn, hence xn+1 = xn/(1 + 4h). Its multiplier lies between zero and one for every positive h in this example. With h = 0.6, the first result is 1/3.4 ≃0.29412, while the exact value is e−2.4 ≃0.09072. The method is stable and positive but markedly inaccurate at this step. The price of the implicit method is solving an algebraic equation at each step. For a vector nonlinear right-hand side f, one must solve z −xn −hf(z) = 0. That inner nonlinear solver has its own stopping rule. A computation may therefore contain temporal discretization error, nonlinear-solve error and floating-point error at the same time. Stiffness describes situations where stability restrictions from fast decaying components force an explicit method to take steps much smaller than the time scale of the output of interest. Consider two independent components with rates −1 and −1000. Even after the fast component is almost zero, explicit Euler still requires a step below approximately 0.002 for its linear stability. The slow component changes on order-one times. An implicit method can address the stability restriction, but its error tolerances must still resolve the slow dynamics and any scientifically relevant fast transient. Keep these separate: 1. model-form error: equations omit or misrepresent reality; 2. parameter/data uncertainty: inputs are imperfectly known; 3. discretization error: continuous equations are approximated on finite time/space grids; 4. floating-point/algorithmic error: arithmetic and iterative solvers are finite precision. Reducing a solver tolerance addresses only part of layer 3/4. It does not validate the model. 5.3 Consistency, stability and convergence For a time-stepping method, local truncation error measures how well one exact solution step satisfies the discrete formula. Consistency means truncation error vanishes as step size goes to zero. Stability means perturbations are not amplified uncontrollably. Under appropriate conditions, consistency plus stability gives convergence. Euler method. For ˙y = f(t, y), yn+1 = yn + hf(tn, yn). Taylor expansion of the exact solution gives y(t + h) = y(t) + hy′(t) + 1 2h2y′′(ξ), so the local error is O(h2) and accumulated global error is O(h). Runge–Kutta idea. Higher-order RK methods combine several slope evaluations to match more Taylor terms without explicitly computing high derivatives. The ubiquitous RK4 is fourth order for sufficiently smooth problems, but adaptive embedded methods are generally preferable in scientific production because they estimate local error and vary step size. 5.3.1 Absolute stability and stiffness Apply a method to the test equation y′ = λy. A one-step method produces yn+1 = R(hλ)yn. Stability requires |R(hλ)| ≤1 for decaying modes. Explicit Euler has R(z) = 1 + z, so for real negative λ it requires −2 < hλ < 0. A fast decaying mode with large |λ| can force tiny steps even if the scientific behavior of interest evolves slowly. This is stiffness. Interpretation: Stiffness is a numerical time-scale mismatch. A stiff system contains stable fast modes that the solution may quickly settle onto, but explicit methods must still take small steps to avoid numerical instability. Implicit methods spend more work per step solving nonlinear/linear systems, but can take much larger stable steps. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

For one-dimensional diffusion ut = Duxx, the central approximation is uxx(xi) ≈ui−1 −2ui + ui+1 h2 . Taylor expansion shows second-order spatial error. Combining this with explicit Euler gives un+1 i = un i + µ(un i−1 −2un i + un i+1), µ = D∆t/h2. Stability requires µ ≤1/2 in 1-D. Refining the spatial grid by two therefore forces explicit time step down by roughly four. This motivates implicit diffusion solvers and operator splitting. Finite volume and conservation. Finite differences approximate derivatives. Finite volume integrates conservation laws over control volumes and balances numerical fluxes through boundaries. For mass conservation ∂tc + ∇· J = R, integrating over volume Vi gives d dt Z Vi c dV = − Z ∂Vi J · n dS + Z Vi R dV. If the same numerical flux is used with opposite sign for neighboring cells, internal fluxes cancel exactly, giving discrete conservation. This is often more important than nominal order for transport models. 5.5 Method of manufactured solutions To verify a PDE solver, choose a smooth manufactured u∗(x, t), substitute it into the PDE, and derive the forcing/boundary data that make it exact. Then grid refinement should recover the theoretical convergence rate. This tests the complete discretization, boundary conditions and solver plumbing. Worked analysis - 2: observed convergence order. If errors at mesh sizes h and h/2 are Eh, Eh/2, estimate pobs = log(Eh/Eh/2) log 2 . A nominal second-order method that consistently gives pobs ≈1 has a defect: perhaps a first-order boundary treatment, an interpolation error or a tolerance that dominates at fine grids. A successful run without an exception is not the same thing. A test can check an analytic value, a conservation law, a shape, an error condition or a convergence pattern. The scientific question determines the expectation; a test framework only organizes its execution and reports the result. The first useful separation is between setup, action and assertion. Setup constructs the inputs. The action calls the function. The assertion states what should be true about its return value. A test that calculates its expected value with the same potentially wrong algorithm as the function under test is often circular. Worked example 1: turn a limiting case into a test For v(s) = V s/(K +s), with V = 10 and K = 2, three expectations can be derived without a numerical solver. Zero substrate gives zero rate. At s = K, the rate is V/2 = 5. At s = 3, the rate is six. The first two are structural properties; the third is a numerical microcase. The pytest assertion for the third case can be written as: 1 import pytest 2 from teaching.core import saturation 73

A vector of three observations has shape (3,). A table of three times and two parameter settings has shape (3, 2). These shapes should encode scientific meaning, not merely satisfy a programming operation. Write down what each axis represents before combining arrays. Broadcasting is a rule that lets arrays with compatible shapes participate in one elementwise operation. NumPy compares dimensions from the right. Dimensions are compatible when they are equal or one of them has size one. A size-one dimension is reused across the other operand. Reuse does not imply that the resulting larger calculation was scientifically intended. Worked example 1: the same values can produce the wrong experiment Let predicted values be p = (1, 2, 3) and observations y = (1.1, 1.9, 3.2). Each prediction corresponds to the observation at the same index. The residual vector is p −y = (−0.1, 0.1, −0.2), X i (pi −yi)2 = 0.06. 85

A function can therefore run, differentiate and optimize successfully while answering the wrong question. The fix is not to prohibit broadcasting. We want all values Xij = e−tikj, with time along rows and parameter setting along columns. Give times shape (3,1) and rates shape (1,2): 1 times = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0]) 2 rates = np.array([0.2, 0.4]) 3 trajectories = np.exp(-times[:, None] * rates[None, :]) 4 assert trajectories.shape == (3, 2) The matrix is approximately X =   1 1 0.81873 0.67032 0.67032 0.44933  . It is not a mysterious vectorization trick; it explicitly marks which quantities are held constant while another dimension varies. A reduction such as a mean removes an axis. X.mean(axis=0) averages across times and returns two values, one per rate. X.mean(axis=1) averages across parameter settings and returns three values, one per time. Those are different summaries. Neither is automatically the desired scientific quantity, and a mean over irregularly spaced times is not a time integral divided by duration. A scalar average noise level would define a different likelihood weighting. For a residual matrix with axes (time, observable), a vector of observable noise scales belongs along the final axis. For noise that varies by time, a different shape is required. A robust API documents the axis convention and checks it. Naming a variable weights does not determine which direction it broadcasts. This distinction carries into sensitivity tensors. An array may have axes (time, observable, parameter). Flattening the first two into rows of a sensitivity matrix is legitimate only if the corre- sponding data and noise scales are flattened in the same order. The examples continue the same modelling and inference threads used elsewhere in the book. ◎Learning objectives • stream evidence records with generators instead of accumulating hidden state; • preserve low-level causes while exposing domain-specific failures; • design reproducible stochastic experiments with explicit random-number streams; • understand why installation, configuration, CLI entry points, and provenance are scientific infrastructure. ☼Pedagogical objective Treat experiment execution as a data-producing pipeline whose failures, seeds, and environment can be reconstructed. ¨ Project link TumorTherapyTwin / StochAgentLab: JSONL evidence records, chained failures, reproducible replicate streams. 9.1 Make a stochastic experiment repeatable without repeating its samples A random-number generator is a deterministic algorithm whose internal state produces a sequence with useful statistical properties. A seed initializes that state. Reusing the same seed reproduces the same sequence; it does not create a new independent experiment. Reproducibility and independent replication are therefore different requirements. A Monte Carlo estimate approximates an expectation with an average over simulated samples. Its sampling uncertainty decreases with the number of suitably independent samples, not with the number of times the same sample is copied. This distinction becomes important when simulations are distributed to parallel workers. Worked example 1: quantify uncertainty in a simulated mean For an exponential lifetime with rate k = 0.4 h−1, the mean and standard deviation are both 1/k = 2.5 h. With N independent lifetimes, the average has variance 2.52/N. At N = 1000, its standard deviation is 91

Ð Chapter 9. Scientific Python IV: Reproducible Experiments, Failures, and Randomness 92 / 413 approximately 0.07906 h. This is the standard error of the mean, not the standard deviation of individual lifetimes. When the population variance is unknown, estimate the standard error as s/ √ N, where s is the sample standard deviation. For a large, well-behaved independent sample, an interval of roughly mean ±1.96 standard errors is a useful normal approximation for the mean. It is not a 95% interval for an individual lifetime, which is much more variable and asymmetrically distributed. The example creates three independent-style child streams and prints each replicate’s estimated mean and standard error. Their numerical means need not equal 2.5. Variation across repeats is expected; demanding exact equality would turn a stochastic test into an almost certain failure. Conversely, accepting any value merely because the computation is stochastic is not meaningful verification. Compare discrepancies to the expected Monte Carlo scale. Worked example 2: restarting one seed creates identical data Consider the following pattern: 1 replicates = [np.random.default_rng(9).normal(size=3) 2 for _ in range(2)] Each iteration constructs a new generator with the same seed. The two arrays are identical. Averaging them does not halve the variance of the estimator. If this pattern is used in parallel workers, a large- looking ensemble may contain repeated copies of a small amount of random information. Instead, create a seed sequence once, spawn child sequences, and attach one to each stable replicate identifier: 1 children = np.random.SeedSequence(2026).spawn(3) 2 results = {i: replicate(child) 3 for i, child in enumerate(children)} A child sequence gives a reproducible way to initialize that replicate’s generator. The library’s spawning mechanism is designed to avoid accidental overlap; it should not be described as a mathematical proof that finite pseudorandom sequences are truly independent. The practical point is to avoid deliberately cloned streams and undocumented state sharing. Execution order must not decide which seed belongs to which replicate. Store identifiers first, then distribute the pairs. If a worker finishes late or a failed job is retried, the same replicate should receive the same child sequence. Combining outputs should also use a deterministic ordering when exact byte reproducibility matters. Worked example 3: common random numbers are an intentional different design Sometimes two model variants should use the same random inputs. Suppose YA = U and YB = U + 0.1, with U random. The difference YB −YA = 0.1 has no sampling variability when the same U is used. Using independent UA and UB adds variability to the comparison. This technique is called common random numbers. It is not a contradiction of independent replication. Within one paired comparison, sharing randomness can reduce the variance of a difference. Across replicate pairs, use new child streams. The design should be stated explicitly: which conditions share randomness, which replicates are distinct, and what quantity is being estimated. Sharing random numbers does not necessarily reduce variance for every nonlinear comparison. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Identifiability asks whether different parameter values can be distinguished by the available observations. A program can return a unique numerical answer because of initialization, parameter bounds or a penalty even when the experiment does not provide a unique scientific answer. We will use one decay model throughout this lesson. It is intentionally small enough that a fit, a sensitivity matrix and a profile can be calculated directly. The point is to learn the procedure before applying it to a much larger biochemical system. Worked example 1: recover an amplitude and a rate from ideal data Let the observed quantity be y(t) = Ae−kt, with unknown amplitude A > 0 and rate k > 0. A has observation units and k inverse-time units. With noiseless observations y(0) = 2 and y(2) = 0.9, the first measurement gives A = 2. Taking the ratio eliminates the amplitude: 0.9 2 = e−2k, k = −1 2 log(0.45) ≃0.399254. The logarithm is applied to a dimensionless ratio. Taking a logarithm of a dimensional measurement without a reference scale obscures its interpretation. This calculation requires a nonzero time separation. With both measurements at time zero, neither says anything about k. With unknown multiplicative sensor gain g, the observations become gAe−kt. Ratios still identify k in this ideal setting, but they identify only the product gA, not g and A separately. That is 105

Chapter 11. Parameter Estimation, Identifiability, and PEtab Workflows 106 / 413 an exact structural ambiguity in this observation specification. Worked example 2: define the noisy fitting problem completely The executable example uses times 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, generating values from A = 2, k = 0.4, and explicitly supplied small perturbations. It assumes independent Gaussian measurement errors with known standard deviation σ = 0.05. The standardized residual at time ti is ri(A, k) = Ae−kti −yi 0.05 , and χ2(A, k) = X i ri(A, k)2. Under the stated Gaussian model, minimizing this sum is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood. The likelihood is the probability density of the observed data viewed as a function of the parameters. It is not itself a probability distribution over the parameters. least_squares receives the vector of residuals, not an already-summed scalar objective. Bounds enforce nonnegative amplitude and rate. The script preserves the observations, the assumed noise scale, the fitted values and the objective. Run python -m teaching.examples.ch11; its measured fit is recorded here: Quantity Value Fitted amplitude 1.984229 Fitted rate 0.390794 Weighted sum of squares 1.178537 The generating parameters are known only because this is a synthetic example. A fit need not recover them exactly after noise is added. In real data the generating values are unknown, so verification has to rely on a broader combination of residual structure, alternative models, independent observations and justified uncertainty analysis. Worked example 3: construct the sensitivity matrix row by row A sensitivity is the derivative of a predicted observation with respect to an unknown. For this model, ∂y(t) ∂A = e−kt, ∂y(t) ∂k = −Ate−kt. At A = 2, k = 0.4, time zero gives the row (1, 0). It directly constrains the amplitude but has no first-order rate information. At time one the row is approximately (0.67032, −1.34064). At time three it is approximately (0.30119, −1.80717). Divide each row by its observation standard deviation to measure changes relative to the expected noise. Stacking the rows gives a matrix with one row per measurement and one column per parameter. Its columns have different parameter units. For a dimensionless comparison, one may use log-parameters, multiplying the amplitude column by A and the rate column by k. State that choice: singular values change when parameter coordinates change. The example compares an early-time design (0, 0.1, 0.2) with a spread design (0, 1, 3) at the same parameters and noise scale. Nearly parallel rows provide little ability to distinguish compensating parameter changes. The saved matrices and singular values make that statement numerically checkable rather than relying on an ellipse drawn by hand. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

For a candidate rate k, set ei = e−kti. The least-squares amplitude has the explicit solution bA(k) = P i eiyi P i e2 i , subject to the nonnegative-amplitude constraint when relevant. Substitute that amplitude back into χ2 to obtain the profile χ2 prof(k). This differs from evaluating the objective at the fitted amplitude for every rate. Freezing the amplitude prevents compensation and can make uncertainty look artificially narrow. The script evaluates 141 rates and saves the reoptimized amplitude at every point. Plot ∆χ2(k) = χ2 prof(k) −χ2 min. A broad flat region indicates that many rates fit almost equally well after compensation. For regular one-parameter likelihood-ratio inference, a cutoff near 3.84 is commonly used for an approx- imate 95% interval. This convention applies to twice the log-likelihood difference, which here equals the change in the standardized sum of squares. It does not automatically apply to an arbitrary loss, a boundary-constrained estimate, a structurally nonidentifiable problem or a small-sample nonregular model. A closed interval on a plot is not a theorem that its coverage is correct. Read the implementation 1 sigma = 0.05 2 truth = np.array([2.0, 0.4]) 3 y = truth[0] * np.exp(-truth[1] * t) + np.array([-0.03, 0.04, -0.02, 0.025, -0.005]) 4 5 def residual(theta): 6 A, k = theta 7 return (A * np.exp(-k * t) - y) / sigma 8 fit = least_squares(residual, [1.0, 0.2], bounds=([0.0, 0.0], [np.inf, np.inf])) 9 grid = np.linspace(0.1, 0.8, 141) 10 profile = [] 11 amplitudes = [] 12 for k in grid: 13 e = np.exp(-k * t) 14 A = max(0.0, float(e @ y / (e @ e))) 15 amplitudes.append(A) 16 profile.append(float(residual([A, k]) @ residual([A, k]))) 17 minimum = float(fit.fun @ fit.fun) 18 designs = {} The loop over candidate rates is the profile calculation. (11.1) An inverse problem starts from observations y and seeks information about p. The inverse map may not be unique or stable even when the forward model is perfectly well defined. 11.3.1 Observation models matter Suppose yi = hi(x(ti; p), p) + ϵi, (11.2) with independent Gaussian noise ϵi ∼N(0, σ2 i ). (11.3) The negative log-likelihood, ignoring constants, is L(p) = 1 2 X i (yi −ˆyi(p))2 σ2 i . (11.4) Thus weighted least squares is not merely a numerical convention; it corresponds to a statistical assump- tion. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Chapter 11. Parameter Estimation, Identifiability, and PEtab Workflows 109 / 413 If variance grows with magnitude, constant-variance Gaussian residuals can be inappropriate. Log-normal or other observation models may better represent measurement mechanisms. 11.3.2 Residual structure After fitting, residuals ri = yi −ˆyi (11.5) should be inspected against time, fitted value, experimental condition, and replicate. Systematic structure suggests missing mechanisms, wrong observation model, or correlated noise. A low total loss can hide strong structured bias. 11.4 Structural identifiability A parameter is structurally identifiable if ideal noise-free, sufficiently rich observations uniquely deter- mine it under the model. Simple example: y(t) = Ae−kt. (11.6) If y(t) is observed continuously and nonzero, both A and k can in principle be identified. But if a model output depends only on product ab, y(t) = f(ab, t), (11.7) then a and b cannot be separately identified from that output: infinitely many pairs with the same product are equivalent. No optimizer or extra precision fixes structural nonidentifiability. You need additional measurements, interventions, constraints, or reparameterization. 11.4.1 Practical identifiability Even structurally identifiable parameters may be weakly constrained by finite noisy data. Practical identifiability depends on experiment design, noise, parameter regime, and sampling times. Symptoms include: • broad confidence intervals/posteriors; • strong parameter correlations; • flat objective profiles; • wildly different parameter values producing similar predictions; • sensitivity columns that are nearly linearly dependent. 11.5 Sensitivity matrix and Fisher information Let predictions be yi(p). Define sensitivity matrix Sij = ∂yi ∂pj . (11.8) Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

(11.9) If F is nearly singular, some parameter combinations are poorly constrained locally. Eigenvectors of F with small eigenvalues identify weak directions in parameter space. 11.5.1 Parameter scaling Sensitivities depend on parameter units. A useful normalized sensitivity is ˜Sij = pj yi ∂yi ∂pj (11.10) when values are nonzero. This dimensionless elasticity measures relative output change per relative parameter change. For positive parameters spanning orders of magnitude, optimize log-parameters θj = log pj (11.11) so positivity is automatic and scales are more balanced. 11.5.2 Local minima and multimodality Nonlinear inverse problems can have multiple minima. A single optimizer run from one initial guess is weak evidence. Use: • multiple starts; • global/local hybrid strategies when needed; • profile likelihood; • posterior sampling; • mechanistically informed parameter bounds. But global optimization does not resolve nonidentifiability. It may simply find many equivalent solutions more effectively. 11.5.3 Synthetic recovery Before fitting experimental data, generate synthetic data from known p∗under the same observation schedule. Ask whether the inference pipeline can recover it. Failure on noise-free synthetic data is a major warning. 11.5.4 Regularization and priors Adding penalty λ∥p∥2 (11.12) can stabilize an inverse problem but changes the estimand. In Bayesian terms, it resembles a Gaussian prior under certain parameterizations. Regularization should reflect plausible structure where possible, not be used only to force the optimizer to behave. 11.5.5 Joint state and parameter estimation When initial conditions or latent states are uncertain, estimating only parameters can bias results. State-space approaches or filtering/smoothing can estimate latent trajectories jointly with parameters. This becomes especially relevant for partially observed dynamical systems. 11.5.6 ML and inverse problems ML can accelerate inverse problems through amortized inference: train a model qϕ(p|y) across simulated parameter-observation pairs. Once trained, inference can be fast. But the network inherits the simulator’s assumptions and training prior. It is not evidence that the mechanistic model is valid. Take a mechanistic model with at least four parameters. Global Sensitivity, Uncertainty Quantification, and Experimental Design 127 / 413 12.7 Experimental design turns sensitivity into action Sensitivity asks what the current experiment reveals; experimental design asks which future observation or intervention would most improve the evidence. In a Gaussian local approximation with sensitivity matrix S and noise covariance Σ, the Fisher information is F = ST Σ−1S. Different design criteria encode different goals. D-optimality maximizes log det F and shrinks the volume of the local uncertainty ellipsoid. A-optimality minimizes tr(F −1) and emphasizes average marginal variance. E-optimality increases the smallest eigenvalue and targets the weakest identifiable direction. These criteria can select different experiments, especially when one parameter combination is much weaker than the rest. The local Fisher matrix is not magic. In nonlinear or multimodal problems it may be a poor approximation to posterior geometry. A useful workflow is therefore hierarchical: screen designs cheaply with local information; simulate synthetic data under the best candidates; then compare profile likelihood, posterior contraction, or decision quality for a smaller set of designs. Design for a scientific decision, not parameter precision by default. The best experiment for identifying every kinetic constant may not be the best experiment for deciding whether a treatment is safe or which genotype is drought tolerant. If the downstream decision depends on g(p) rather than p itself, propagate uncertainty to g and design around uncertainty in that quantity. This connects experimental design directly to Chapter 18: information has value because it can change a decision. A practical design report should therefore state: candidate interventions/times/sensors; cost or feasibility constraints; assumed noise model; criterion; weak information directions before and after design; and a simulation-based stress test showing what happens if the nominal parameter point is wrong. A prior describes that uncertainty before incorporating the current observations. A likelihood describes how the observed data would arise at each candidate parameter value. Their product, after normalization, is the posterior. These are roles in a model, not three interchangeable curve names. For a continuous parameter, the posterior is a density. Its value at one point is not the probability that the parameter equals that exact point. Probabilities are obtained by integrating over regions. Before using a sampler or an ODE likelihood, we will perform two analytic updates, separate parameter uncertainty from observation variation, and then work through a filter update and a small sampling example. Worked example 1: infer a probability from ten trials Suppose ten conditionally independent trials produce seven successes and three failures. Let p be the success probability. Ignoring a multiplicative factor that is constant in p, the likelihood is p7(1 −p)3. A beta prior with parameters (2, 2) has density proportional to p2−1(1 −p)2−1 on 0 < p < 1. Multiplying prior and likelihood gives p(p | data) ∝p8(1 −p)4, so the posterior is beta(9, 5). Its mean is 9/(9 + 5) = 9/14 ≃0.642857. The raw observed success fraction is 7/10 = 0.7. The posterior mean lies between that fraction and the prior mean 1/2 because both sources of information contribute. 128

Worked example 4: the scalar Kalman update is Gaussian conditioning Suppose a model predicts a scalar state with mean 10 and variance four. A measurement is 13 with noise variance one. Its fluctuations are not necessarily numerical error. A deterministic mean equation and a stochastic event model can describe different aspects of the same system. The quantity of interest determines which description is needed: a mean population is not an extinction probability, and a smooth average is not a waiting-time distribution. A hazard is an instantaneous event rate conditional on the event not having occurred yet and on the current state. Its units are inverse time. A hazard of two per hour is not a probability of two. For a short interval ∆t, the event probability is approximately 2∆t; an exact finite-interval formula requires the process assumptions. Worked example 1: derive the exponential waiting time If the event hazard is a constant a, let S(t) be the probability of no event by time t. Over a small additional interval, S(t + ∆t) ≃S(t)(1 −a∆t). Dividing the change by ∆t gives S′(t) = −aS(t) with S(0) = 1. Hence S(t) = e−at, and the waiting-time cumulative probability is 1 −e−at. To sample a waiting time, set a uniform random variable U equal to the survival probability and solve U = e−aT : T = −log U a . For a = 1.5 h−1 and U = 0.5, T ≃0.462098 h. A rate of zero means no event occurs; it must be handled as an absorbing no-event case rather than divided into the logarithm. With multiple reaction channels, total hazard is the sum a0 = P r ar. Sample the waiting time using a0, then choose channel r with probability ar/a0. Recalculate all state-dependent hazards after the event. Scientific objectives can be discontinuous, stochastic, simulation-based, event-driven or produced by legacy software with no derivatives. Global structure may contain multiple basins. Derivative-free methods are therefore essential, but they are also easy to misuse: a heuristic returning a low number is not evidence of global optimality. When not to use derivatives. Derivative-free optimization is justified when: • the simulator is a black box; • branch/event logic creates nonsmoothness; • Monte Carlo noise overwhelms finite differences; • variables include categorical/discrete choices; • gradients are too expensive relative to function evaluations. If reliable autodiff exists for a smooth problem, derivative-free search usually wastes information. Nelder–Mead and pattern search. Nelder–Mead moves a simplex through reflection, expansion, contraction and shrinkage. It is intuitive and often useful for small smooth problems, but has limited guarantees and scales poorly with dimension. Pattern-search methods evaluate structured poll directions and can have stronger convergence properties for nonsmooth objectives. Powell/model-based methods. Modern derivative-free optimization often builds local interpolation models of the objective and updates a trust region. This recovers some curvature information from function values. For expensive low/moderate-dimensional simulations, such methods can outperform naive population heuristics. Evolutionary/global heuristics. Differential evolution, CMA-ES and related methods maintain populations and balance exploration/exploitation. Simulated annealing accepts occasional uphill moves with temperature-dependent probability. They are useful for multimodal or rugged objectives but require many evaluations and provide weak global guarantees in finite time. 18.2 Multistart as a scientific baseline A surprisingly strong baseline is: sample many initial points using Latin hypercube/Sobol designs, run a robust local optimizer, cluster final solutions and compare objective values. Repeat random algorithms across seeds. Report distribution of best-found objective versus evaluation budget. Include feasibility rate and wall-clock if parallelism differs. Its parameters are adjusted to reduce a loss that measures disagreement with training targets. A forward pass computes predictions. Backpropagation applies reverse-mode differentiation to compute how the loss changes with parameters. An optimizer uses those derivatives to update the parameters. They are three separate operations. Adding more layers does not remove the need to understand one complete gradient calculation. We use a single hidden unit with a smooth activation, then construct a counterexample showing why small prediction error can coexist with poor scientific derivatives. Worked example 1: compute a forward pass and loss Let z = wx + b, h = tanh z, by = ah, L = 1 2(by −y)2. Here x is an input, y the target, w a weight, b a bias and a an output weight. The hyperbolic tangent maps a real number to (−1, 1) and has derivative 1 −tanh2 z. The loss is one half the squared error so its derivative with respect to the prediction is simply by −y. For x = 1, y = 0.8, w = 0.5, b = −0.2 and a = 1.5, we get z = 0.3, h ≃0.291313, by ≃0.436969, and error approximately −0.363031. The prediction is too low. The next question is which parameter changes raise it in a way that reduces this loss. 232

Software engineering is presented as scientific change control: architecture, contracts, tests, and interfaces preserve meaning. 24.2 Scientific software architecture follows scientific change vectors A trustworthy package is organized around what must remain stable when scientific questions change. Separate domain equations, numerical algorithms, observation models, inference procedures, I/O, and presentation. This is dependency control in service of epistemic clarity: changing a plotting library should not change the model; changing a solver should not silently change units or observation definitions. Treat validation as part of the public API. Shape, units, parameter domains, solver status, finite outputs, and convergence evidence should fail loudly. Numerical tests should include invariants and reference problems, not only function-level unit tests. The goal is not maximal abstraction; it is to make scientific assumptions and computational failure visible at interfaces. 24.3 Architecture begins with scientific responsibilities Architecture is not a folder aesthetic. It is the set of decisions that determines which parts of a scientific program can change independently. For a computational model, useful responsibilities often include: • model definition: equations, parameters, state variables, units, constraints; • numerical execution: integration, root finding, optimization, sampling; • inference: residuals, likelihoods, priors, estimation procedures; • analysis: derived quantities, sensitivity metrics, stability analysis; • I/O: configuration, datasets, result serialization; • presentation: plots, reports, notebooks, web interfaces; • orchestration: choosing a model, method, configuration, and execution path. A frequent research-code defect is that these responsibilities are fused into one function. A simulation routine reads a CSV, mutates global parameters, solves an ODE, generates a figure, and saves it to disk. That function is hard to test because its scientific core cannot be exercised without also invoking unrelated I/O and plotting behavior. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Repro- ducibility means these dependencies can be recovered well enough to rerun and inspect the result. It is distinct from scientific correctness: a reproducible wrong equation remains wrong. It is also distinct from exact byte identity: different valid numerical environments may agree to a scientifically appropriate tolerance without producing identical bytes. A useful record allows another person to answer four concrete questions: what was run, with which inputs, in which environment, and what result should be compared? The following examples make these requirements operational. Worked example 1: a configuration hash identifies bytes, not meaning Take the configuration rate=0.4, time=2.0, initial=1.0. The example serializes its dictionary with sorted keys and fixed JSON separators, then computes a SHA-256 digest of those exact bytes. Sorting prevents a harmless change in dictionary insertion order from changing this chosen serialization. A hash changes when the bytes change. It does not say whether the rate is per second or per hour, whether the initial amount is measured or assumed, or whether the code implements the intended equation. Those meanings belong in the data schema and documentation. A run record therefore needs both machine identifiers and human-readable scientific context. A manifest lists file paths and hashes. To verify a release, check every listed file, check for missing entries and check for unlisted distributed files. Verifying only the ZIP’s ability to open is a different 316

Æ Chapter 25. Performance, HPC, Reproducibility, FAIR, and Deployment 317 / 413 integrity check. A package can be uncorrupted yet contain an obsolete PDF, stale version metadata or an inaccurate figure. Worked example 2: derive the idealized parallel speedup limit Suppose a fraction p of a workload can be divided perfectly across N processors, while fraction 1 −p must remain serial. If one-processor time is normalized to one, ideal time is (1 −p) + p/N. Speedup is therefore S(N) = 1 (1 −p) + p/N . For p = 0.9, four processors give S(4) = 1/(0.1 + 0.225) ≃3.07692. Even infinitely many processors cannot exceed ten under this model, because the serial tenth remains. For p = 0.99, the ideal ceiling is 100. The example plots these calculated bounds for stated parallel fractions. It does not invent runtime measurements. Actual communication, synchronization, input/output, memory limits and load imbalance can reduce observed speedup. Some changed algorithms also change the work itself, so their speedup should not be interpreted using an unchanged-work bound without qualification. Worked example 3: a benchmark must keep the scientific task fixed Comparing two solvers at different tolerances does not isolate implementation speed. A faster run may simply return a less accurate result. Match the quantity of interest and an appropriate accuracy criterion, then record runtime, memory where relevant, problem size and environment. Warmup, caching and compilation can also change what is being timed. For a parameter sweep, total runtime can include failed runs and uneven evaluation costs. Report how those were handled. Removing every failure from a timing table can make an unreliable method look efficient. A reproducible benchmark should retain both successful and failed run records with clear status. In stochastic comparisons, use declared independent or paired random streams and enough repetitions to assess sampling variation. A runtime measured once can be dominated by unrelated system activity; a numerical difference measured once can be dominated by random input variation. Worked example 4: distinguish a development environment from a release environment An environment file records dependencies, but its presence does not prove those dependencies were installed or tested together. Record actual versions from the execution environment and retain the command output of successful tests. A clean-install test should start outside the source directory and should not inherit an undocumented PYTHONPATH. An archived notebook with saved outputs provides a useful record, but it may depend on hidden execution order. A fresh execution from a clean kernel tests that ordering. If notebooks are preserved rather than re-executed, say so. Do not convert an inherited output into a fresh validation claim by changing a version label. The script python -m teaching.examples.ch25 prints the configuration serialization, its digest and the speedup arrays. The package’s release script separately regenerates a complete manifest and verifies the archived PDF against the standalone PDF. These are mechanical release checks; scientific tests and visual inspection are reported separately. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

It helps to separate at least four questions. Repeatability: Can the same person rerun the same code in essentially the same environment and recover the result? Computational reproducibility: Can another person reconstruct the software environment, inputs, parameters, and commands and recover the numerical result? Robustness: Does the scientific conclusion survive reasonable changes in numerical method, imple- mentation, random seed, preprocessing, or hyperparameters? Replication: Does independent evidence or a new experiment support the scientific claim? A container may improve computational reproducibility while doing nothing for replication or conceptual robustness. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Therefore, “requirements.txt exists” is not the same as “the experiment is reproducible.” A practical hierarchy is: 1. declare compatible dependencies in pyproject.toml; 2. create a resolved environment or lock file for a specific experiment or release; 3. record platform metadata at runtime; 4. preserve exact input data identifiers or hashes; 5. store the Git commit and configuration with outputs. Dependency declaration versus locking. A library should usually declare ranges broad enough to coexist with other packages. An application or published computational experiment can be stricter. For example, a reusable package might state: requires-python = ">=3.11" dependencies = ["numpy>=2.0", "scipy>=1.14"] while the exact environment used for a publication may record the resolved versions. Why not pin every transitive dependency in the library metadata? Because that can make depen- dency resolution unnecessarily rigid for downstream users. The software artifact and the experimental environment serve different purposes. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

A file called measurements. csv can change while keeping the same name. A cryptographic hash detects byte-level changes. 1 from hashlib import sha256 2 from os import PathLike 3 from pathlib import Path 4 5 6 def file_sha256(path: str | PathLike[str]) -> str: 7 """Return the SHA-256 digest of a readable file using bounded memory.""" 8 file_path = Path(path) 9 if not file_path.is_file(): 10 raise FileNotFoundError(f"cannot hash missing file: {file_path}") 11 digest = sha256() 12 with file_path.open("rb") as handle: 13 for block in iter(lambda: handle.read(1024 * 1024), b""): 14 digest.update(block) 15 return digest.hexdigest() For large scientific datasets, use a versioned data store or manifest rather than copying everything into Git. Randomness is an input. A stochastic computation is not “unreproducible by nature.” Randomness can be made explicit. Prefer passing a generator: 1 from numpy.typing import NDArray 2 import numpy as np 3 4 5 def simulate(n_steps: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> NDArray[np.float64]: 6 """Generate a reproducible stochastic trajectory from a caller-owned RNG.""" 7 if not isinstance(n_steps, int) or n_steps < 1: 8 raise ValueError(f"n_steps must be a positive integer; got {n_steps!r}") 9 if not isinstance(rng, np.random.Generator): 10 raise TypeError("rng must be numpy.random.Generator") 11 noise = rng.normal(size=n_steps) 12 return np.cumsum(noise) 13 14 15 rng = np.random.default_rng(42) 16 result = simulate(1000, rng) Avoid scattering calls to global random state throughout modules. Æ Chapter 25. Performance, HPC, Reproducibility, FAIR, and Deployment 322 / 413 Therefore decide what reproducibility level you need. Bitwise identity can be useful for debugging, but scientific reproducibility often means agreement within justified numerical/statistical tolerances. Parallel reduction and non-associativity. Real arithmetic is associative: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). (25.1) Floating-point arithmetic is not exactly associative. A parallel sum may combine partial sums in a different order from a serial sum, causing small differences. For well-conditioned quantities this is harmless. For unstable calculations it can expose deeper problems. If changing thread count changes the scientific conclusion, the conclusion is numerically fragile. 25.3.3 Reproducible workflows A useful experiment command should be declarative: python -m mechlab.run --config configs/figure_3.toml The command should create an output directory containing: results/figure_3/ config.toml provenance.json metrics.json trajectory.parquet figure.pdf A future researcher should not need to execute notebook cells in an undocumented order. Caching without lying to yourself. Caching expensive computations is valuable, but cache keys must include every input that can affect the result. A cache keyed only by parameter vector may be invalid if solver tolerance, model version, or dataset has changed. A robust cache key can be derived from a canonical serialized configuration plus code/model version. If you cannot state the full dependency set, cache invalidation is unsafe. Failure to watch. The most dangerous reproducibility failure is a stale result that looks legitimate. Silent reuse of cached data or old notebook state can preserve a figure after the code that generated it has changed. Notebooks and hidden state. A notebook may produce different output depending on cell execution history. Before release: 1. restart the kernel; 2. execute all cells from top to bottom; 3. ensure it imports installed project modules rather than relying on path hacks; 4. avoid storing large hidden state that is not generated in the notebook or loaded explicitly; Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

A scientifically meaningful commit should answer one question. Examples: • “Correct sign of product inhibition term in Eq. 7.” • “Add BDF solver option without changing default numerical behavior.” • “Refactor result serialization; reference trajectories unchanged.” • “Update parameter values to dataset v3 and regenerate calibration benchmark.” A commit called “many fixes” hides whether the mathematical model changed. Separate kinds of change. When possible, do not combine these in one commit: 1. mathematical-model change; 2. numerical-method change; 3. refactor with intended identical behavior; 4. dependency upgrade; 5. formatting/UI change; 6. data update. The separation is not bureaucratic.
