It can change which scientific analyses are feasible. A tenfold simulation speedup may enable global sensitivity analysis, Bayesian inference, larger ensembles, real-time model exploration, or higher spatial resolution. But premature optimization can make code complex without changing the dominant cost. The first rule is: measure →explain →change →measure again. (25.2) Start with complexity. If an algorithm scales as O(n3), optimizing a constant factor may not help once n grows. Before low-level tuning, ask whether the algorithmic formulation is appropriate. Examples: • dense linear solve: roughly O(n3), while sparse structure may reduce practical cost dramatically; • all-pairs distances: O(n2) memory/time, potentially avoidable with spatial indexing; • naive parameter grid with k values in d dimensions: kd, an exponential curse of dimensionality; • Monte Carlo standard error: O(N−1/2), so 100 times more samples only reduces error by a factor of 10. A better algorithm usually beats micro-optimization. 25.8.1 Profile the real workload Microbenchmarks can identify local cost, but start with application-level profiling. In Python, useful tools include the standard profiler, line profilers, memory profilers, and framework-specific profilers. The critical questions are: • What fraction of wall time is spent in each function? • Is execution CPU-bound, memory-bound, I/O-bound, or waiting on external resources? • Are many temporary arrays allocated? • Is the solver spending time in RHS evaluations, Jacobians, linear solves, or event handling? • Does runtime scale with states, samples, mesh size, or parameter dimension as expected? Large intermediate arrays can increase memory traffic and allocation. For y = ax2 + bx + c, (25.3) a naive expression may create several temporaries. Whether this matters depends on array size and frequency. Memory layout and cache behavior. Modern CPUs are much faster at arithmetic than at fetching uncached memory. Contiguous access patterns matter. NumPy arrays are typically row-major (C-order) unless specified otherwise. Operations along contiguous dimensions often perform better. Transposed views may be non-contiguous; some libraries silently copy them, which can dominate runtime. Inspect: 1 print(x.shape, x.strides, x.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"]) For large simulations, memory footprint can determine whether a computation is feasible at all. Sparse structure. Many mechanistic models have sparse Jacobians because each equation depends on only a subset of states. Exploiting sparsity can accelerate stiff ODE integration, nonlinear solves, and optimization. If the Jacobian J ∈Rn×n has O(n) rather than O(n2) nonzero entries, storing and factorizing it densely wastes both memory and computation. The performance lesson is scientific: understand interaction structure before choosing linear algebra. Compiled loops and JIT. Some algorithms are difficult to vectorize: event-driven simulation, agent updates, irregular loops, recursive calculations. Options include: • Numba-style JIT compilation; • JAX compilation when the computation fits its functional array model; • Cython or native extensions for stable low-level kernels; • compiled libraries exposed through Python. Use the simplest tool that solves the bottleneck. A 20-line compiled kernel wrapped by clear Python may be preferable to rewriting an entire scientific project in a lower-level language. GPU computing: arithmetic intensity matters. GPUs excel when many similar operations can run in parallel and enough computation occurs per byte transferred. They are less effective for tiny models, branch-heavy logic, repeated CPU–GPU transfers, or algorithms dominated by serial dependencies. A basic performance model is: time ≈max  operations compute throughput, bytes moved memory bandwidth  . (25.4) Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Performance regressions. A test suite can protect performance if runtime matters. Avoid brittle hard cutoffs on shared CI machines. Prefer relative benchmarks, trend tracking, or coarse thresholds designed to catch order-of-magnitude regressions. 25.8.3 Accuracy–cost tradeoffs Scientific performance is rarely “fastest wins.” Compare cost for a target error. If method A takes 1 s with error 10−3 and method B takes 3 s with error 10−7, the meaningful comparison depends on required accuracy. Plotting error versus runtime across resolutions often reveals which method is efficient for the scientific target. Worked analysis. For an ODE model, compare RK45 and BDF across tolerances. Record runtime, RHS evaluations, and error relative to a high-accuracy reference. A stiff model may show BDF slower at loose accuracy but dramatically better at stringent accuracy. The conclusion “solver X is faster” is incomplete without the accuracy regime. Optimization can change semantics. Replacing sequential agent updates with fully vectorized simultaneous updates can define a different stochastic process. Reordering floating-point reductions can change tiny results. Using lower precision can affect stiff solvers or likelihoods. Every performance change to a scientific kernel therefore needs an equivalence test appropriate to the model. Choose one expensive modelling workflow and obtain at least a 3–10x speedup without changing its scientific output beyond justified tolerance. Document baseline profile, intervention, final profile, accuracy comparison, hardware, and the new analysis that the speedup makes feasible. 25.9 Parallelism is a property of the computation A workload is parallelizable when parts of it can be computed independently or with limited coordination. These are often embarrassingly parallel: each task can run without communicating with the others until aggregation. By contrast, a tightly coupled PDE solve on a distributed mesh requires frequent communication and is a more difficult parallel problem. 25.9.1 Amdahl’s law 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 Processor count 100 101 Idealized speedup Parallel fraction 0.5 Parallel fraction 0.9 Parallel fraction 0.99 Ideal linear speedup Figure 25.3: Idealized Amdahl speedup for fixed parallel fractions, with no communication or scheduling overhead. The curves are analytic limits, not measured runtime. The serial fraction sets an upper bound even with arbitrarily many workers. If fraction p of a workload can be parallelized and fraction 1 −p is inherently serial, ideal speedup on N workers is S(N) = 1 (1 −p) + p/N . (25.5) As N →∞, Smax = 1 1 −p. (25.6) If 10% is serial, no number of workers can exceed a 10x speedup under this model. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Threads versus processes in Python. Python threads share memory, but CPU-bound pure-Python code is constrained by the interpreter’s global lock in standard CPython. Many NumPy/SciPy operations release that lock because computation occurs in native code, so threading can still help in some cases. Processes have independent Python interpreters and memory spaces. They avoid the global lock but incur serialization and memory overhead. For independent heavy simulations, processes are often straightforward: 1 from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor 2 from numpy.typing import ArrayLike, NDArray 3 import numpy as np 4 5 6 def run_one(theta: ArrayLike) -> NDArray[np.float64]: 7 """Run one independent parameter scenario for process-level parallelism.""" 8 parameters = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float) 9 if parameters.ndim != 1 or not np.all(np.isfinite(parameters)): 10 raise ValueError(f"theta must be a finite 1D vector; got shape {parameters.shape}" ) 11 return np.asarray(simulate(parameters), dtype=float) 12 13 14 with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool: 15 results = list(pool.map(run_one, parameter_sets)) However, if each process invokes a multithreaded BLAS library, eight processes may each spawn eight threads and oversubscribe the machine. Control thread counts intentionally. Task granularity. Parallel tasks should be large enough that scheduling, serialization, and process startup are small relative to computation. If each model run takes 1 ms, submitting each as an individual remote cluster job is inefficient. Batch many model evaluations into one task. If each run takes 20 minutes, one run per task may be appropriate. A useful efficiency metric is η = S(N) N . (25.7) Low efficiency indicates overhead, imbalance, contention, or serial work. Load imbalance. Scientific tasks can have unpredictable runtimes. Some parameter sets may make an ODE stiff, cause an optimizer to take many iterations, or terminate early. Static assignment can leave one worker busy while others are idle. Dynamic task queues improve utilization. On clusters, job arrays can be split into chunks of roughly comparable expected cost. Parallel random-number streams. Never seed every worker with the same integer; that can produce identical stochastic trajectories. Modern random-number systems support creating independent child streams from a seed sequence. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Shared memory and data locality. Copying a multi-gigabyte dataset to every process can erase any speedup. Strategies include: • memory-mapped arrays; • shared-memory blocks; • reading data once per worker rather than once per task; • partitioning data so workers process local chunks; • using distributed object stores/frameworks when justified. Data movement often dominates distributed computing. Always estimate bytes transferred, not only floating-point operations. 25.9.2 SLURM mental model On many HPC systems, you do not run expensive work directly on the login node. You request resources from a scheduler. A simplified batch script: #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=sobol #SBATCH --time=02:00:00 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8 #SBATCH --mem=16G #SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out source .venv/bin/activate python -m mechlab.sensitivity --config configs/sobol.toml Important resource concepts: node: physical machine; CPU/core: execution resource on a node; task: usually a process/rank; CPU per task: threads/cores assigned to one process; memory: typically requested per job/node/task depending on scheduler options; Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Requesting excessive resources can increase queue time and waste allocation; requesting too little causes failure or poor performance. 25.9.3 Job arrays for parameter sweeps A job array submits many similar jobs indexed by an integer. Each array index can select a subset of parameters. #SBATCH --array=0-99 python -m mechlab.batch --chunk $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID The mapping from chunk index to scientific inputs must be deterministic and stored so results can be reconstructed. Checkpointing. Long simulations should recover from interruption. A checkpoint should record enough state to resume safely, including model state, iteration number, RNG state if relevant, and algorithm metadata. Do not confuse checkpointing with saving a final result. Checkpoints are operational artifacts and may have stronger compatibility requirements. MPI and tightly coupled parallelism. Message Passing Interface (MPI) is appropriate when processes need explicit communication. Typical operations include broadcasts, reductions, point-to-point messages, and collective synchronization. You do not need MPI for every HPC task. For independent parameter sweeps, job arrays or process pools are often simpler. Learn MPI when the scientific algorithm requires distributed state or when a specialized solver already uses it. 25.9.4 Parallel scaling experiments Measure both strong scaling and weak scaling where relevant. Strong scaling keeps total problem size fixed while increasing workers. Weak scaling increases problem size proportionally with workers. Report speedup and efficiency, not merely runtime on the largest machine. Failure to watch. Parallelism can make bugs nondeterministic and harder to reproduce. Race condi- tions, unordered aggregation, duplicated seeds, oversubscription, and partial failures should be expected engineering concerns, not surprises. Convert one expensive sensitivity, bootstrap, or ensemble workflow into an HPC-ready pipeline. Include local execution, parallel execution, deterministic chunking, checkpoint/restart, provenance, and a scaling benchmark. This is strong evidence for scientific-software roles. 25.10 Data structures are part of the model A column called rate without unit, measurement context, uncertainty, and meaning is not a complete scientific variable. Tidy tables versus labeled multidimensional arrays. Tabular data is ideal when observations can be represented as rows and variables as columns. Multidimensional simulation fields are often better represented as labeled arrays with explicit dimensions. For example, a climate-model output may have dimensions scenario × time × latitude × longitude × variable. (25.9) Flattening this into a CSV can lose dimension semantics and be inefficient. Choose representation based on access pattern and dimensional structure. CSV is not a database or array store. CSV is portable and readable, but weak for: • data types; • missing-value conventions; • large files; • random access; • multidimensional data; • embedded metadata; • compression. Columnar formats such as Parquet are efficient for large tables. HDF5, NetCDF, or Zarr-style stores can represent multidimensional scientific arrays. Databases help when querying relational records or coordinating concurrent access. No format is universally best. 25.10.1 Schemas prevent accidental interpretation Define what columns and fields must exist, their types, ranges, and units. Do not log sensitive data or enormous state arrays by default. Health versus correctness. A health endpoint returning “200 OK” means the service process responds. It does not mean the science is correct. A deeper readiness check can run a tiny reference computation and verify a known invariant or bench- mark. Keep it cheap enough for operational use. Scientific API versioning. If a result schema or model semantics change, version the API explicitly. /v1/ can remain stable while a /v2/ endpoint introduces new semantics. Scientific platforms frequently accept equations, expressions, uploaded files, or model definitions. Treat these as untrusted input. Risks include: • arbitrary code execution from eval; • path traversal in uploaded filenames; • denial of service through huge computations; • malicious archives; • unsafe serialization formats; • dependency vulnerabilities. If users submit mathematical expressions, parse an allowed grammar rather than evaluating arbitrary Python. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Worked investigation 2: fit the wrong observation model as a controlled failure First deliberately set the assumed gain to one. For each candidate k, calculate standardized residuals (by(ti; k) −yi)/0.03 and minimize their squared sum over a declared positive interval. Observation assumption Fitted rate χ2 Gain 1 (deliberately wrong) 0.298401 15.9285 Gain 0.85 (generating value) 0.400078 0.7777 This is an informative comparison because only one assumption changed. The wrong gain can be partially compensated by a changed rate, but the time-dependent pattern need not disappear. Worked investigation 3: calculate a posterior without hiding it inside a sampler For the corrected observation model, specify a uniform prior on k ∈[0.2, 0.65]. Evaluate the Gaussian log likelihood on a fine uniform grid. Subtract its maximum before exponentiating, then normalize the weights. Because grid spacing is constant, its common factor cancels in normalized expectations. The posterior mean is the weighted average of grid rates. Its variance is the weighted average squared deviation from that mean. The grid is a numerical quadrature approximation, so check that refinement and extension of the parameter domain do not change the reported result materially. It is not a replacement for a high-dimensional sampler; it is a transparent small-dimensional reference. Now ask for a future sensor observation at time four. For every candidate rate, calculate the predicted mean and the Gaussian probability that the new observation exceeds 1.3. Average that conditional probability over posterior weights. This integrates parameter uncertainty and future observation noise rather than substituting only the fitted rate. Posterior/predictive quantity Value Mean rate 0.400522 Rate standard deviation 0.010793 P(ey(4) > 1.3 | y) 0.956207 The probability is conditional on the stated model, prior interval, known total, known gain and noise model. It is not a validated risk estimate for an empirical system. The calculation nevertheless teaches exactly where uncertainty enters a decision quantity. The slab ignores heterogeneous vasculature, cell-level variation, advection, and changing tissue geometry. At steady state, a key dimensionless competition is between consumption and diffusion. In the low-concentration linearized regime q ≈ (Vmax/Km)c, the steady equation becomes d2˜c d˜x2 −ϕ2˜c = 0, ϕ2 = VmaxL2 DKm . If only steady normalized profiles are observed and the system remains in the linear uptake regime, doubling Vmax and D together leaves ϕ2 unchanged. The normalized shape is nearly unchanged. Verification checks whether a calculation implements its stated mathematical problem adequately. Validation examines whether the model is suitable for its intended use in the world. Worked example 2: report a failed assumption as a result The coupled heat example uses exact scalar subsolvers but shows a nonzero error in the combined state and energy balance. The correct conclusion is not “the scalar solver is broken.” It is that the partitioned exchange schedule introduces an error that decreases under refinement. The same reporting pattern transfers to solver tolerance, mesh spacing, observation timing or a surrogate’s training domain. In an optimization study, a search that finds no candidate satisfying all constraints supports a statement about the tested model, candidate set and search effort. Naming the exact scope prevents both exaggeration and unnecessary dismissal of useful work. Worked example 3: distinguish three kinds of uncertainty in one sentence Suppose a simulation reports an estimated extinction probability from repeated paths. There is Monte Carlo uncertainty from finite simulation, parameter uncertainty from incomplete knowledge of rates, and model uncertainty from the choice of process. A confidence interval based only on the number of simulated paths addresses the first component. A precise statement would say: “The interval reflects finite-simulation variability conditional on the fixed pure-death model and stated rate.” It should not be described as total uncertainty about the survival of a real cell population. More simulated paths reduce Monte Carlo error but do not repair a missing birth process or an incorrect observation mechanism. This is also why a narrow parameter interval or a high cross-validation score cannot stand alone. Explain which sources of uncertainty were included, which were excluded and which could alter the decision. A.13 Practice 7A: singular covariance The matrix is vvT with v = (2, 1)T , so zT Pz = (vT z)2 ≥0 for every z. It is positive semidefinite, with eigenvalues five and zero. The direction (1, −2)T has zero variance. A Cholesky implementation requiring strict positive definiteness need not accept this singular matrix; the validity of a covariance and the preconditions of a particular factorization are distinct questions. A.14 Practice 7B: a valid float can be an invalid request The negative time is a model-domain failure, not a parsing failure. The API declares nonnegative time, so runtime validation should reject it before simulation. A return value of type float would establish only its representation. It would not establish that evaluating a backward-time process is within the supported scientific contract. A.15 Practice 8A: reductions remove an axis Averaging the replicate axis, axis one, changes shape (50, 4, 3) to (50, 3): one mean for each time and species. Averaging the species axis instead gives (50, 4) and combines species values. That may be inappropriate when species have different units, roles or biological meanings. A sum or weighted combination could be justified by a conservation law, but it must be defined scientifically rather than chosen because it produces a convenient shape. A.16 Practice 8B: matched noise weights Standardized residuals are (0.2/0.1, −0.3/0.3) = (2, −1). Their squared sum is 4 + 1 = 5. The residual function should return shape (2, ) for two matched observations, not an accidental (2, 2) all-pairs matrix. The noise vector should use the same observation ordering. A.17 Practice 9A: sample size for a mean Require 2.5/ √ N ≤0.05. Squaring gives N ≥(2.5/0.05)2 = 2500. This calculation assumes indepen- dent samples with the stated standard deviation. Correlation or a heavier-tailed distribution can change the precision achieved by a raw sample count. A.18 Practice 9B: repeated copies are not extra replication There are only 100 independent paths. Their average has standard error proportional to 1/ √ 100 = 1/10, not 1/ √ 10000 = 1/100. A naive calculation treating every copy as independent underestimates the standard error by a factor of ten. Duplicating saved paths changes storage size, not the amount of random information. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

The result record should include model name, rate 0.5, time 2, initial state 3 and this prediction. A negative rate or nonfinite input should be rejected under the declared contract and produce a nonzero command exit status, not a success record with an arbitrary fallback number. A.20 Practice 10B: import success is environment-dependent One possibility is missing or incorrect package-discovery metadata, so the built distribution omitted the module. Another is code that reads a relative file path assuming the repository is the current directory. Install a non-editable copy into a temporary environment or target, switch to an unrelated directory, and run an import plus the reference command. Inspect the imported module path to avoid accidentally exercising the source checkout. A.21 Practice 11A: ideal exponential recovery Time zero gives A = 1.2. The ratio 0.6/1.2 = 0.5 = e−2k gives k = (log 2)/2 ≃0.346574 per time unit. An unknown multiplicative sensor gain would confound the absolute amplitude: the data identify gain times amplitude, not each factor separately. The time ratio still identifies the rate under this ideal model. A.22 Practice 11B: repeats at zero do not observe the rate The sensitivity row at zero is (∂y/∂A, ∂y/∂k) = (1, 0). Repeating that row improves amplitude precision but leaves the rate column zero and the matrix rank one. A measurement at positive time adds a nonzero rate sensitivity. Its usefulness depends on timing, noise and the other observations; merely saying “more data” does not specify the information gained. A.23 Practice 12A: no interaction For independent uniform inputs, total variance of X1 + X2 is 2/3. Each main-effect variance is 1/3, so S1 = S2 = 1/2. There are no interactions, hence total indices equal the first-order indices. Their sum is one because every variance contribution belongs to exactly one input. A.24 Practice 12B: timing and heteroscedastic noise With constant observation noise and known amplitude, the information optimum is t = 1/k = 5. If standard deviation is σ(t), the log-information derivative is 2/t −2k −2σ′(t)/σ(t). Its root need not remain at five. Growing measurement noise can make a later-time observation less valuable than the constant-noise calculation suggests. A.25 Practice 13A: a beta update A beta(1, 1) prior contributes exponents zero and zero. Four successes and two failures add those counts, giving posterior beta(5, 3). Its mean, and the predictive success probability for one new conditionally independent trial, is 5/8 = 0.625. The observed fraction is 4/6, so the posterior mean is mildly shrunk towards the prior mean one half. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Ç Appendix A. Worked solutions to the teaching-path practice problems 379 / 413 A.26 Practice 13B: trust the noisier observation less The gain is K = 1/(1 + 4) = 0.2. Innovation is three, updated mean is 10 + 0.2(3) = 10.6, and updated variance is (1 −0.2)1 = 0.8. The observation is relatively noisy, so the estimate moves less than in the earlier example with gain 0.8. The update follows the stated variances; it is not a subjective adjustment after seeing the result. A.27 Practice 14A: extinction with three individuals Expected extinction time is (1 + 1/2 + 1/3)/0.5 = 11/3 ≃3.66667. By time two, each individual has died with probability 1 −e−1. Independence gives extinction probability (1 −e−1)3 ≃0.25258. The mean population at that time, 3e−1, is a different quantity and is not an extinction probability. A.28 Practice 14B: stationarity is distributional The stationary distribution is Poisson with parameter 3/0.6 = 5, so mean and variance are five. A path frozen at five has variance zero across time or an ensemble of identical copies and never performs immigration or death events. It is not a realization of the stationary jump process, even though its constant value equals the stationary mean. A.29 Practice 15A: a case that does not distinguish implementations From (S, I, S), both endpoint agents see the infected middle agent, so the synchronous result is (I, I, I). Sequential order one, two, three also gives (I, I, I) because the infected middle agent remains infected and can transmit to both endpoints. This case is useful for checking the local rule but not for detecting the scheduling difference. The earlier (I, S, S) case is more discriminating. A.30 Practice 15B: finite-interval probability Total hazard is 3(0.1) = 0.3 per minute. For fixed neighbours over two minutes, event probability is 1 −e−0.6 ≃0.451188. The linear approximation gives 0.6, noticeably higher. Using it as an exact probability would change the model. If neighbours can change during the interval, the fixed-hazard calculation itself becomes conditional or approximate. A.31 Practice 16A: capacity-weighted equilibrium Initial thermal content is 2(8) + 6(0) = 16 in the common units. At equilibrium, (2 + 6)T ∗= 16, so T ∗= 2. The unweighted average four is wrong because the colder reservoir has three times the heat capacity. The calculation assumes no external heat exchange and constant capacities. A.32 Practice 16B: a steady leaf balance The sensible heat flux is 180 −100 = 80 W m−2. Dividing by 16 W m−2 K−1 gives a leaf–air difference of five kelvin. During a rapid transient, non-negligible heat storage requires a heat-capacity term such as C dTl/dt; setting the balance instantaneously to zero would omit it. Worked solutions to the teaching-path practice problems 380 / 413 A.33 Practice 17A: a nonzero gradient at a constrained optimum The unconstrained minimizer is three, but the feasible interval ends at two. Thus x∗= 2. With g = x −2 ≤0, L = (x −3)2 + λ(x −2). Stationarity at two gives −2 + λ = 0, so λ = 2. The positive multiplier and active boundary satisfy complementary slackness. A.34 Practice 17B: curvature controls the step interval The derivative is 10(x −1). The error recurrence is en+1 = (1 −10η)en. Convergence requires |1 −10η| < 1, giving 0 < η < 0.2. The objective has greater curvature than (x −2)2, so the same step can be too aggressive. A universal learning rate cannot be justified independently of the problem’s scale. A.35 Practice 18A: weights depend on scale With w = 0.75, u∗= 1 −w = 0.25 and the objective pair is (0.0625, 0.5625). If the first objective is multiplied by 100, the derivative of the weighted sum gives u∗= (1 −w)/(100w + 1 −w) = 0.25/75.25 ≃0.00332226. The numerical weight is unchanged but the implied preference is not. Units and normalization must therefore be reported. A.36 Practice 18B: improvement from uncertainty When fmin = µ, z = 0 and the first expected-improvement term vanishes. The result is σϕ(0) = σ/ √ 2π. It is positive for positive uncertainty and tends to zero as uncertainty vanishes. A candidate whose mean merely matches the current best can still be useful because its uncertain value might improve it. A.37 Practice 19A: preserve the grouping unit There are 8(4) = 32 rows. Six training plants give 24 training rows; the other two give eight test rows. Plant-identifier overlap must be zero for this new-plant evaluation. Splitting individual rows randomly would answer a different question if repeated measurements carry plant-specific information. A.38 Practice 19B: costs determine the threshold The threshold is 3/(3 + 1) = 0.75. At p = 0.6, predicting positive has expected error cost 3(0.4) = 1.2, while predicting negative costs 1(0.6) = 0.6. Under these costs, negative has lower expected loss. This calculation presumes that the probability is meaningful for the deployment population and that the stated costs capture the decision consequences. A.39 Practice 20A: a full gradient at zero activation With z = 0, h = tanh 0 = 0, prediction is zero and loss is 1/2. Error is −1 and activation derivative is one. Hence ∂L/∂a = (−1)0 = 0, ∂L/∂w = (−1)(1)(1)(2) = −2, and ∂L/∂b = −1. Changing the input to two makes the weight and bias gradients distinct. Ç Appendix A. Worked solutions to the teaching-path practice problems 381 / 413 A.40 Practice 20B: derivative errors amplify frequency The function perturbation is bounded by 0.01. Its first derivative is 0.5 cos(50x), bounded by 0.5. Its second derivative is −25 sin(50x), bounded by 25. A small-amplitude high-frequency error can therefore be almost invisible in a state plot and severe in a derivative-based scientific calculation. A.41 Practice 21A: identical net dynamics Pairs (k, a) = (0.3, 0.1) and (0.6, 0.4) both give a −k = −0.2, hence the same trajectory e−0.2t from one. An independent measurement of the removal flux kx at a known nonzero state can determine k; the net trajectory then determines a. More measurements of only the same state trajectory cannot break this exact compensation. A.42 Practice 21B: one flux, two balance entries The derivatives are ˙x1 = −0.6 and ˙x2 = 0.6, so the total derivative is zero. With independently learned derivatives, a mismatch such as −0.6 and 0.58 gives total derivative −0.02, an unexplained loss. Sharing the same flux with opposite signs enforces the modeled conservation identity at the equation level. A.43 Practice 22A: recover carrying capacity from coefficients The equation is ˙x = 0.6x −0.2x2, so the four-term coefficient vector is (0, 0.6, −0.2, 0)T . The nonzero equilibrium is −0.6/(−0.2) = 3. Its interpretation as a carrying capacity depends on the logistic model and the observed regime; a fitted coefficient ratio alone is not proof of a population mechanism. A.44 Practice 22B: differentiation magnifies noise The central-difference noise variance is σ2/(2h2). Doubling the standard deviation multiplies σ2 by four. Halving h divides h2 by four, introducing another factor four. The combined variance increase is sixteen, and the corresponding standard deviation increases by four. A.45 Practice 23A: three distinct retrieval metrics Two of four retrieved documents are relevant, so precision at four is 1/2. Two of the four relevant documents are retrieved, so recall at four is 1/2. The first relevant item appears at rank two, giving reciprocal rank 1/2. These values happen to agree numerically; their denominators and meanings differ. A.46 Practice 23B: preserve the requested calculation Without recorded arguments, a reviewer cannot tell whether a finite output used the requested rate or an inherited default. A regression test should call the tool with two explicit rates at the same nonzero time, verify both returned argument records, and compare each result with its own analytic exponential. Testing only the default rate would not expose the hardcoding defect. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Worked solutions to the teaching-path practice problems 382 / 413 A.47 Practice 24A: different tests for different layers At A = B = 1 and k = 0.3, derivatives are (−0.3, 0.3) and sum to zero. A balance test checks that cancellation. The sensor gives 0.8(1) + 0.1 = 0.9, checked by an observation-reference test. Passing the balance test would not detect a sensor implemented with gain one instead of 0.8. A.48 Practice 24B: stale state versus wrong parameters One defect is a cached result not invalidated by the changed parameter. Another is a plotting routine that reruns the model with a hardcoded default instead of using the current result. Record the actual parameter dictionary, configuration hash, run identifier and raw state/observation arrays returned to the plot. If the numeric result changes but the display does not, the fault lies later in the rendering path; if parameters never reach the solver, it lies earlier. A.49 Practice 25A: a serial fraction remains Ideal time is 0.2+0.8/8 = 0.3, so speedup is 1/0.3 = 10/3 ≃3.33333. With infinitely many processors, the parallel term vanishes and the ceiling is 1/0.2 = 5. Real overhead can reduce speedup below this idealized unchanged-work calculation. A.50 Practice 25B: source identity is not run identity Different input data, configurations or random streams can change outputs with identical source code. Dependency versions, hardware arithmetic and parallel reduction order can also matter. Expected floating-point differences may be acceptable when they lie within a justified scientific tolerance and preserve conclusions. Different units, missing data or altered parameter values are not explained away as harmless numerical variation. A.51 Practice 26A: the observation map changes the number At time two, B = 2(1−e−0.8) ≃1.101342072. The calibrated sensor prediction is 0.85B ≃0.936140761. The unit-gain model returns 1.101342072. Their difference is approximately 0.165201311, caused by the observation assumption, not by the kinetic state solver. A.52 Practice 26B: the product is identified, not its factors Replacing (g, M) by (cg, M/c) leaves gM(1 −e−kt) unchanged for every nonzero admissible c. Ob- servations in that same channel cannot separate the two factors, regardless of the number of sampling times. An independent total-amount measurement or a calibrated sensor standard can fix one factor and make the other estimable under the remaining assumptions. A.53 Practice 27A: narrow the claim to the evidence A defensible replacement is: “The surrogate fitted the stated in-domain training data and passed the specified conservation check on the tested cases. These results do not establish derivative accuracy, extrapolation performance, satisfaction of all physical constraints or empirical validity.” This statement retains the useful evidence while identifying the missing tests. It does not infer broad physical correctness Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Ç CHAPTER B Research investigations: diagnostic guid- ance This appendix pairs the 44 investigations with guided resolutions. Some remain methodological guides rather than fully closed numerical analyses. The revised chapters and executable studios supply the completed reference cases explicitly identified there, including the four-stage tumour investigation. Open these only after an attempt; do not equate a checklist with a completed scientific result. B.1 Chapter 1: cumulative investigation walkthroughs Investigation 1.1: Model reconstruction without copying Return to the investigation. Task. Using only the biological assumptions above, derive all four right-hand sides. For every term, write: process, sign, units, and one limiting-case test. Diagnostic guidance for the open investigation. Step 1: Start by drawing four rows N, L, T, u and three columns source/sink/interaction. Step 2: Derive each term from the prose before looking at the published equation. Step 3: For T, logistic growth gives cT(1-dT); pairwise killing gives -alpha2 NT and -beta2 LT; drug toxicity gives -kT uT. Step 4: Repeat for N and L, then u’=v-omega u. Step 5: Check units term-by-term. Step 6: The decisive verification is not a matching trajectory: set u=0, T=0, and N=L=u=0 in separate tests and confirm that the corresponding mechanisms disappear. Step 7: A correct submission includes at least one failed test created by deliberately flipping a sign, because that demonstrates the test can detect the defect rather than merely pass the final implementation. State one dataset or intervention that could discriminate the two formulations, and explain why ordinary trajectory fit may not be sufficient. Diagnostic guidance for the open investigation. 384

Step 2: At low u, the Emax model is approximately -(kmax/EC50)uT, so ordinary data concentrated in this regime cannot distinguish the two forms; they are locally confounded. Step 4: The discriminating evidence is curvature/saturation at high concentration, not an improved optimizer score on the same narrow-dose trajectory. Ç Appendix B. Research investigations: diagnostic guidance 387 / 413 Investigation 4.1: Sensitivity-equation derivation Return to the investigation. Task. Derive the full sensitivity ODE for one chosen parameter of the four-state tumor model and verify it against finite differences. Diagnostic guidance for the open investigation. Step 1: For x’=f(x,theta), define s_j=dx/dtheta_j and differentiate: s_j’=f_x s_j+f_theta_j with s_j(0)=d x0/dtheta_j. Step 2: Apply this to one tumor parameter, writing every nonzero derivative explicitly. Step 3: Integrate x and s_j together. Step 4: Verify against centered finite differences over a logarithmic h sweep; error should decrease at O(h^2) before roundoff rises. Step 5: One h value is not evidence. Step 6: If the sensitivity and finite difference disagree only at loose ODE tolerances, the derivative may be correct while the forward solve is contaminating the check. Simulate the birth–death system with SSA and show convergence of stationary mean and variance to the analytic Poisson result as ensemble size grows. Diagnostic guidance for the open investigation. Step 1: For birth rate lambda and death rate mu n, the stationary distribution is Poisson(lambda/mu); both mean and variance equal lambda/mu. Step 2: Run independent SSA trajectories long enough to approach stationarity, discard burn-in, and estimate mean/variance across increasing ensemble sizes. Step 3: Plot error versus number of replicates with uncertainty. Step 4: The target is convergence to the analytic moments within Monte Carlo error. PF.1 Parametrized scientific tests Step 1 - identify the experiment table. The two optimization algorithms are different experimental cases even if they share the same acceptance criterion. Step 2 - parameterize the test. 1 from functools import partial 2 import numpy as np 3 import pytest 4 5 @pytest.mark.parametrize( 6 "label,solver", 7 [ 8 ("local", solve_rosenbrock_local), 9 ("global", partial(solve_rosenbrock_global, seed=3)), 10 ], 11 ) 12 def test_rosenbrock_finds_reference_minimum(label, solver): 13 result = solver() 14 assert result.success, f"{label} solver did not converge" 15 assert np.linalg.norm(result.x - np.ones(2)) < 2e-3 16 assert result.fun < 1e-8 Step 3 - create a fresh fixture. 1 @pytest.fixture 2 def tumor_params() -> Params: 3 return Params(v=1.8, omega=0.9) The fixture function is called separately for each dependent test. Ç CHAPTER E Final competence standard The final standard is not the number of algorithms remembered. It is the ability to enter an unfamiliar scientific problem and construct a defensible chain: expose assumptions, choose a representation, verify the computation, connect observations to latent quantities, construct an inference or learning protocol, quantify uncertainty, design diagnostics that can falsify the pipeline, engineer the work as maintainable software, and state precisely what the evidence does and does not support. 411
